---
title: "Figure 16.1: LAC: Share of FDI Global Greenfield Investment"
---

![Python: `python/fig-16-1.py`](../images/python/fig-16-1.png)

The region's share of global greenfield FDI, measured in two ways: by
capital expenditure (how much money is announced) and by number of projects
(how many investments are announced). Both are three-year trailing moving
averages, so each point is the average of that year and the two before it.
The moving average is already in the data; the script draws the numbers as
they are.

This is about as plain as a line chart gets: two series, annual data, one
y-axis, a legend. It is a good page to read after
[Figure 1.1](fig-1-1.qmd) to check that you can follow a whole script on your
own.

**New in this chart:** a subtitle on two lines.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 21 rows (2005 to 2025):

| category | Capital expenditure | Project-count |
|---|---|---|
| 2005 | 8.35 | 5.59 |

The `category` column holds the years as numbers (2005, 2006, ...), not as
text. That matters: matplotlib can then place them on a numeric x-axis, so
you can set the axis limits in years and choose which years get a label.
Compare [Figure 2.4](fig-2-4.qmd), where the categories are quarters such as
`2022Q1` and must be plotted at positions 0, 1, 2, ... instead.

## The script

### The colours

```python
series_colours = {"Capital expenditure": "#0066A6", "Project-count": "#C8580A"}
```

A dictionary that links each column name to its colour. The colours are
written as hexadecimal codes, the same codes Excel shows under *More colours
→ Custom → Hex*. Using the column names as keys means the loop below can
read both the data and the colour from the same entry, and the legend labels
come out as the column names.

### The frame and a two-line subtitle

```python
fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="LAC: Share of FDI Global Greenfield Investment",
    subtitle="(Percent of world total; three-year trailing moving\naverage)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Orbis Crossborder Investment (OCBI) database; and IMF staff\n"
        "calculations.\n"
        ...
    ),
    left=0.35,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.3,
)
```

The subtitle is too long for one line, so it contains a `\n`, Python's code
for a line break. The break is placed where the published chart breaks the
line, after "moving".

You do not have to make room for the second line yourself. `new_chart()`
counts the `\n` in the title and subtitle and moves the top of the plot down
by one line height for each. The same goes for the caption at the bottom,
which here has six lines: the plot simply starts higher. See [The shared
layout](../chart-style.qmd#sec-new-chart).

The three spacing arguments are in inches:

- `left=0.35` leaves room for the y-axis labels (at most two digits here);
- `right=0.15` is a small margin on the right, since there is no right-hand
  scale;
- `bottom_gap=0.3` is the space between the caption and the x-axis, enough
  for the year labels.

### The lines

```python
for series, colour in series_colours.items():
    ax.plot(data["category"], data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.9,
            solid_capstyle="round", label=series)
```

The loop runs twice, once per entry in `series_colours`. Each time,
`ax.plot()` draws one line: the years on the x-axis, the column `series` on
the y-axis.

- `linewidth=1.9` is in points, like Excel's line width.
- `solid_capstyle="round"` gives the line rounded ends, as Excel does. The
  matplotlib default is a square end. See [Line
  styles](../techniques.qmd#sec-line-styles).
- `label=series` stores the name for the legend. Without it,
  `ax.legend()` would have nothing to show.

### The x-axis

```python
ax.set_xlim(2004.5, 2025.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(2005, 2026, 5))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=2.8, pad=5)
```

- **The limits** start half a year before the first point and end half a
  year after the last. The lines then do not touch the edges of the plot.
- **The labels.** `range(2005, 2026, 5)` gives 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025.
  In Python, a range stops *before* its end value, so the end is 2026 to
  include 2025. Only these years get a tick mark and a label.
- **The tick marks** are 2.8 points long, and `pad=5` puts 5 points between
  the tick and its label. See [Tick marks and axis
  lines](../techniques.qmd#sec-ticks).

### The y-axis and the legend

```python
set_y_scale(ax, 4, 16, 2)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.04, 0.98), handlelength=3.0,
          labelspacing=0.15)
```

`set_y_scale(ax, 4, 16, 2)` is the shared helper for a y-axis from 4 to 16
with a tick every 2 (4, 6, ..., 16), the equivalent of setting minimum,
maximum and major unit in Excel's *Format Axis* pane. See [The
y-scale](../chart-style.qmd#sec-y-scale).

The legend is placed by its top-left corner (`loc="upper left"`) at the
point `bbox_to_anchor=(0.04, 0.98)`. These numbers are fractions of the plot
area: 4 percent from the left, 2 percent below the top. Two other arguments
tune its look:

- `handlelength=3.0` makes the line sample in the legend three font sizes
  long, a little longer than the default, as in the published chart;
- `labelspacing=0.15` puts the two entries close together.

See [Legends](../techniques.qmd#sec-legends).

The script ends with `save_chart(fig, STEM)`, which writes
`python/figures/fig-16-1.png`.

## Changing the chart

- **A new data year.** If the next edition adds 2026, extend the x-limits to
  `2025.5 → 2026.5` and, if you want 2026 labelled, the range to
  `range(2006, 2027, 5)` or another set of years.
- **A third series.** Add a column name and colour to `series_colours`. The
  loop and the legend pick it up automatically.
- **A one-line subtitle.** Remove the `\n`. The plot grows by one line
  height without any other change.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-16-1.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-16-1.py"}
"""Figure 16.1: LAC: Share of FDI Global Greenfield Investment."""
from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart, set_y_scale

STEM = "fig-16-1"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)

series_colours = {"Capital expenditure": "#0066A6", "Project-count": "#C8580A"}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="LAC: Share of FDI Global Greenfield Investment",
    subtitle="(Percent of world total; three-year trailing moving\naverage)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Orbis Crossborder Investment (OCBI) database; and IMF staff\n"
        "calculations.\n"
        "Note: Shares are computed on announcement years relative to all\n"
        "destination economies in the database and cover announced and\n"
        "completed projects. Latest available data as of September 2, 2026. FDI =\n"
        "foreign direct investments; LAC = Latin America and the Caribbean."
    ),
    left=0.35,
    right=0.15,
    bottom_gap=0.3,
)

for series, colour in series_colours.items():
    ax.plot(data["category"], data[series], color=colour, linewidth=1.9,
            solid_capstyle="round", label=series)

ax.set_xlim(2004.5, 2025.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(2005, 2026, 5))
ax.tick_params(axis="x", length=2.8, pad=5)

set_y_scale(ax, 4, 16, 2)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=2.8)

ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.04, 0.98), handlelength=3.0,
          labelspacing=0.15)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
